summary: Defines a media-level attribute for the Session Description Protocol called content. A sender can attach it to media streams to say more about what the stream contains, beyond what the media line says.

eli5.summary: A call description says a stream is video. This adds a label that says what the video shows, such as a slide presentation or a speaker, so receivers can pick which stream to show.

subtitle: A small SDP attribute that tells a receiver whether a video stream is slides, the speaker or sign language.

tldr.problem: When a session description contains several similar media streams, such as three video streams, the receiving application cannot tell from the media line what each one shows.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4796 defines a media-level SDP attribute, 'content', whose values (slides, speaker, sl, main, alt, or registered extras) label what a stream contains.
tldr.outcome: Applications can lay out or route streams automatically, but the RFC does not define what they must do with the labels, and a peer that ignores the attribute still sets up the session.

today: RFC 4796 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Labels
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP, see RFC 4566) describes multimedia sessions and is often used with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261). Sometimes one application receives several media streams that look alike in the description, for example two video streams. Their m= lines do not say what each stream shows.

RFC 4796 adds a media-level attribute named content that gives more detail than the m= line. The main purpose is to let applications take automated actions based on it. The RFC does not define those actions, so two implementations can behave quite differently when they receive the same attribute.
sections.eli5: When there are several videos that all look the same on paper, a label tells the computer what is in each one.

sections.title: Motivation and Existing Alternatives
sections.content:
SDP had no way to describe the content of a stream (speaker's image, slides, sign language) in a form an application can understand. A person can see the stream, but the application cannot. In the RFC's example, slides, the speaker and sign language travel as separate streams, and the application should place each in the right part of its screen without the user rearranging them for every session. A second example is an application controlling an auditorium with a main screen, two smaller screens, main speakers and headsets: the user could choose outputs once and have them reused for later sessions.

The RFC explains why existing tools do not fit. The label attribute (RFC 4574) has an unrestricted namespace already used in application-specific ways, so part of it cannot be reserved. Using label as a pointer into an external document works only where such documents exist, such as centralized conferencing. The i attribute is meant for humans, not for automata.
sections.eli5: Existing name tags were either already used for other things, needed a separate sheet of paper, or were written for people instead of computers. So a new tag was made.

sections.title: The Content Attribute and Its Values
sections.content:
The attribute is written a=content: followed by one or more comma-separated values. A value is one of the pre-defined words or an extension token. A sender MAY attach it to any media stream it describes.

  • slides: presentation slides, for example in online seminars and courses. Similar to the presentation role in H.239.
  • speaker: the image of the speaker, as video or a still image.
  • sl: sign language, for example an audio stream translated into sign language sent over video.
  • main: a stream from the main source, such as a camera on the performer at a concert.
  • alt: a stream from an alternative source, such as ambient sound separated from the main sound. Similar to the live role in H.239.

All values can be used with any media type. An application can decide how to handle a stream from both its media type and its content value. If it has no special logic for a combination, it uses its default handling for that media type. The same value can appear more than once in a session description.
sections.eli5: There are five ready-made name tags: slides, speaker, sign language, main and alternative. You can stick any of them on any kind of stream.

sections.title: Use in Offer/Answer and Announcements
sections.content:
The attribute is only informative in the offer/answer model (RFC 3264). There is no way to discover whether the peer understands it, and a peer that does not understand it still establishes the session. The only consequence is that the user on that side may have to direct the streams by hand.

The attribute describes what the sender of the description intends to send on that stream. Values for the two directions need not match. An answer MAY contain content attributes even if the offer had none, and MAY omit them even if the offer had them. The attribute can also be used in declarative SDP, such as descriptions distributed with the Session Announcement Protocol (RFC 2974).
sections.eli5: The tag is just a hint. If the other side cannot read it, the call still works, and the person simply sorts the streams themselves.

sections.title: Examples and SMIL
sections.content:
The first example describes three H.261 video streams, each with one value: slides, speaker and sl. The second puts two values on one stream, a=content:slides,speaker, plus sl on a second stream. The RFC notes that a conferencing system might then automatically mix the presenter and slides video.

The values can also be used with the Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL), whose param element also gives an application-specific description of media content. How to combine the two is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: One stream can wear two tags at once, like Slides and Speaker, which tells the system it could blend them together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker may add, modify or remove content attributes in a session description. Depending on how an implementation reacts, this could make an application behave in an undesirable way, so integrity protection of SDP session descriptions is strongly RECOMMENDED. For SDP carried in SIP, S/MIME or Transport Layer Security (TLS) can provide it.

The RFC assumes the values carry nothing truly harmful if exposed, and the initial values need no confidentiality protection. S/MIME and TLS can provide it if needed.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could swap the name tags and make the wrong video show up, so the messages should be sealed so nobody can change them.

sections.title: IANA Registry for Content Values
sections.content:
The RFC registers the content attribute as a media-level attribute that is not subject to charset. IANA created a subregistry for its values under the SDP Parameters registry, with the five initial values above. New values need Specification Required.

New values should consist of a meta description of what a stream contains. They should not describe what to do to handle a stream.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps track of all allowed name tags. New tags should say what a stream is, not what to do with it.

a=content:slides,speaker
